summary: Nvidia chips pile up in Hong Kong as Beijing slows imports and DeepSeek reportedly turns to Huawei; shoppers save before Double 11; AI-made short dramas boom.
body: About 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are waiting in Hong Kong because Beijing has not approved large imports into mainland China, Reuters reports, citing people familiar with the matter[^1]. Only some have been let in, and an eight-chip H200 server now sells in China for over 6 million yuan (about US$900,000), roughly three times last year's price[^1]. Reports say China wants its companies to run AI on Chinese chips instead[^1][^2]. In the same direction, DeepSeek, the Chinese AI lab, reportedly plans to train its next model, V5, on Huawei's Ascend chips, according to unnamed industry sources; neither company has confirmed it[^3][^4]. My read: Beijing is accepting slower AI progress now in exchange for less dependence on US technology later.

Many shoppers are holding back before Double 11 (November 11), China's biggest online sale. Retail sales grew just 1.1% in the first three quarters, and second-hand home prices in 100 cities fell 6.7% from a year earlier in October[^5]. Instead of spending, many families are paying off mortgages early: staff at three state banks in Shanghai say early repayments are above 2 billion yuan a month at each bank, against about 100 million three years ago[^5]. Spending on services is growing faster than spending on goods[^6].

Daily life: short dramas, series of one- or two-minute vertical episodes watched on phones, are booming. China's TV regulator says nearly 550,000 were released in the first ten months of 2026, about 17 times last year's total, and Caixin reports most new releases were made with AI[^7]. ByteDance's short-drama app Hongguo reached 430 million users in September[^7].
differences: Only one outlet, DIGITIMES, says DeepSeek's training on Huawei chips would happen in 2027 on the Ascend 950; the original report, carried by TechNode, gave no timeline[^3][^4].
